analysis.one_liner: Bans factories from dumping plastic pellets into the nation's waterways.
analysis.headline: The bill was introduced with 65 cosponsors and referred to committee, where it awaits action with no hearing or vote.
analysis.plain_summary: Plastic pellets—the tiny raw beads melted down to make plastic products—regularly spill from factories and wash into rivers, lakes, and the ocean. This bill would order the EPA, within 60 days of passage, to issue a rule banning those discharges from any facility that makes, uses, packages, or transports pre-production plastic, and to write that ban into the facilities' water permits. It has not advanced beyond its committee referral.
analysis.who_benefits: Everyone who uses or lives near the nation's waters: the bill would stop plastic pellets—raw plastic beads that factories spill into rivers, lakes, and coastal waters, where they harm fish and wildlife and work their way into the food supply. Fishing, tourism, and waterfront communities would see less pellet pollution; households avoid the costs of cleanup and contaminated waterways.

how_it_helps.text: It requires the EPA to write a final rule prohibiting facilities that make, use, package, or transport plastic pellets from discharging those pellets into U.S. waters.
The prohibition must be written into all wastewater and stormwater permits and performance standards covering those facilities, so the limit is enforceable rather than voluntary.

analysis.who_pays: Plastic manufacturers, plastics molding and forming plants, and companies that package or ship plastic pellets, who would have to contain and treat their wastewater and runoff to meet a zero-discharge rule; some of those costs could pass into plastic product prices.

drawbacks.text: The bill gives EPA only 60 days after enactment to issue a final rule prohibiting the discharges, a very tight timeline that could produce a rushed rule or invite legal challenges over compliance costs.

A flat prohibition on pellet discharge gives facilities little flexibility about how to comply, and the compliance costs—containment equipment, monitoring, permit changes—will be passed into the prices of plastic goods.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefits—less plastic pollution in the nation's waters—are broad and public, while the costs fall on a narrow set of plastic manufacturers who would have to contain their material. The main design risk is that a rigid discharge ban might be costly for smaller facilities to comply with, since the bill sets a short deadline for EPA to finalize rules. On balance the bill's benefits are diffuse and public, its costs concentrated.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and sent to the House Transportation and Infrastructure Committee, which sent it to a subcommittee, and no further action has been taken.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on February 12, 2026 and referred to the House Committee on Transportation and Infrastructure.
The next day it was referred to the Subcommittee on Water Resources and Environment, where it has sat without a hearing, markup, or floor vote.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: If the bill stalls, plastic producers benefit because they avoid new containment and discharge-control requirements; the public has gained nothing yet.

for.name: Rep. Mike Levin
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Plastic Pellet Free Waters Act and recruited the original cosponsors.

sides.party_line_note: All 65 cosponsors are Democrats, and the bill sits in committee controlled by the House's Republican majority, which has not acted on it.

industries.note: The bill would prohibit plastic pellet discharges from facilities that make, use, package, or transport pre-production plastic, requiring containment and treatment measures. Compliance costs fall on the industry; the benefit of cleaner waterways is spread across the public.

industries.industry: Plastic molding, forming, and transport companies
industries.note: These point sources would face new permit limits and containment obligations under the bill. Costs would be modest relative to revenues but real, particularly for smaller facilities.

analysis.trajectory: The bill sits in the Water Resources and Environment Subcommittee with no hearing or markup scheduled and no Republican cosponsors. Most bills at this stage in the minority party never reach the floor, so its likely path is to expire at the end of the Congress unless leadership decides otherwise.
